  "title": "TTRA: Critic-Guided Test-Time Retrieval-Augmented RL for Domain-Adaptive Autoformalization",
  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization models—even those achieving strong in-distribution results (ATF: 94.51% Pass@1 on FormalMath-Lite; ATLAS: 96.93% pass@128 on miniF2F)—degrade sharply on unfamiliar mathematical domains because they lack both domain-specific Mathlib knowledge and mechanisms to adapt at deployment time. Test-time RL (TTRL) has been shown to boost informal math reasoning dramatically but cannot be naively applied to autoformalization: (1) majority voting over formal statements is ill-defined (unlike numerical answers), requiring a trained semantic critic; (2) GRPO's advantage normalization amplifies noise from ambiguous pseudo-labels in the multi-tier reward setting (compilation + critic + BEq); and (3) static retrieval of Mathlib dependencies becomes stale as the formalizer's behavior shifts during adaptation, yet no prior work fine-tunes the retriever during test-time RL. Can we make TTRL viable for autoformalization by combining compilation-error-driven co-adaptive retrieval that exploits Lean 4's full structured error taxonomy, a calibrated semantic critic reward, and principled adaptation of binary-reward debiased RL to multi-tier rewards?",
  "opportunity": "Four independently validated capabilities have never been combined: (1) Co-adaptive retrieval is newly feasible, and identifier hallucination is a quantifiably dominant error mode. R3 (NeurIPS 2025) demonstrates that RAG environment feedback can train retrievers via reinforced contrastive learning. Reinforced-IR (ACL 2025) validates alternating retriever-generator mutual adaptation through RLRF/RLGF. TTARAG (arXiv 2601.11443, Jan 2026) shows test-time retrieval adaptation is achievable via self-supervised prediction. Critically, DDR (arXiv 2511.11990) quantifies that ICL-based dependency generation produces ~30% hallucinated (non-existent) Mathlib identifiers, while retrieval-based DDR reduces hallucination to <2% (Hall_m=0.016). The RAutoformalizer (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) explicitly classifies compilation errors into 'Hallucination' (errors caused by hallucination of identifiers) and 'Others', establishing identifier hallucination as a primary error class worthy of dedicated treatment. MathAtlas (May 2026) further shows a 66% performance advantage for Mathlib-grounded definitions (27.9% vs 16.8% correct, p<0.001), confirming that dependency availability is the critical bottleneck. Yet no work applies co-adaptive retrieval to Lean 4 dependency retrieval during RL-based autoformalization—where Lean's structured error taxonomy (unknownIdentifier, type mismatch with type signatures, failed to synthesize with typeclass names, unknown namespace) provides a graded hierarchy of machine-parseable signals for retriever training. (2) TTRL with debiasing has advanced rapidly. DDRL (ACL 2026 Findings) fixes GRPO's spurious signal amplification via frequency-based balanced sampling, fixed +/-1 advantages, and consensus-based off-policy refinement, achieving up to 19.0% relative improvement over ETMR on AIME 2024 (9.2pp absolute: 15.8 to 25.0 for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B). But DDRL assumes binary correct/incorrect rewards. GDPO (NVIDIA, arXiv 2601.05242, Jan 2026) addresses multi-reward GRPO through per-reward decoupled normalization, preventing reward signal collapse. The combination—binarize multi-tier rewards for DDRL's debiasing, then enrich with GDPO's per-reward normalization for continuous components—has not been attempted. (3) CriticLean (July 2025) provides the missing reward signal: CriticLeanGPT-14B-RL achieves 84.8% accuracy on CriticLeanBench (87.0% for the 32B variant), raising autoformalization pipeline accuracy from 54% to 84% over compilation-only feedback. However, CriticLeanBench evaluates on a balanced 250-correct/250-incorrect distribution, while OOD TTRL produces heavily skewed distributions (often <10% compilable candidates). This distributional shift gap has not been characterized, motivating our Phase 0 calibration protocol. (4) Online RL for Autoformalization (Wang et al., NeurIPS 2025 MAR Workshop) validates RL for autoformalization (TC1: 17.29% to 26.01% on RLMEval using GRPO with composite BEq + embedding rewards), but operates at training time with labeled/unlabeled data on in-distribution problems, without retrieval, test-time adaptation, or a trained semantic critic. Recent infrastructure (DDR's 500K-sample dependency dataset, CRAMF's 26K Mathlib concept index, FormalMATH's multi-domain benchmark, MathAtlas's 52K graduate-level problems with 178K dependency relations, Kimina Lean Server, open-source CriticLeanGPT models) makes the combined approach newly feasible.",
  "landscape": "The landscape spans five relevant lineages. (1) RL for autoformalization: FormaRL (COLM 2025) applies GRPO with compilation + LLM consistency rewards, improving pass@1 from 4% to 26% on ProofNet. Online RL for Autoformalization (Wang et al., NeurIPS 2025 MAR Workshop) uses GRPO with composite rewards (BEq + embedding-based similarity) for Lean 4, achieving TC1: 17.29% to 26.01%, TC50: 76.41% to 85.46% on RLMEval—the closest prior work but operates at training time on in-distribution problems, uses embedding similarity rather than a trained semantic critic, and lacks retrieval and test-time adaptation. ReForm (2026) applies position-aware RL rewards for reflective autoformalization (+22.6pp average). (2) Semantic critics and iterative refinement: CriticLean (July 2025) introduces CriticLeanGPT, with the 32B-RL variant achieving 87.0% accuracy and the 14B-RL variant reaching 84.8% on the balanced CriticLeanBench (250 correct, 250 incorrect). The paper reports TPR, FPR, TNR, and FNR metrics but evaluates only on balanced distributions, leaving the heavily skewed OOD regime uncharacterized. ATF achieves 94.51% Pass@1 on FormalMath-Lite via SFT + expert iteration + DPO with multi-LLM consistency checking. Monotonic Refinement achieves 90.27% composite on miniF2F through multi-model ensemble orchestration. These achieve impressive results but cannot adapt model weights to new domains. (3) Debiased RL and multi-reward optimization: DDRL (ACL 2026 Findings) addresses GRPO's spurious signal amplification through three components: frequency-based balanced sampling excluding ambiguous samples, fixed +/-1 advantages, and consensus-based off-policy refinement—achieving up to 19.0% relative improvement over ETMR on AIME 2024. Critically, DDRL operates exclusively with binary rewards and its authors note that 'more expressive advantage formulations' are left for future work. GDPO (NVIDIA, arXiv 2601.05242) addresses multi-reward GRPO through per-reward decoupled normalization, demonstrating that standard GRPO collapses distinct reward combinations into identical advantage values. (4) Co-adaptive retrieval: R3 (NeurIPS 2025) optimizes retrieval for RAG via reinforced contrastive learning. Reinforced-IR (ACL 2025) alternates RLRF and RLGF for mutual adaptation. TTARAG (arXiv 2601.11443) demonstrates test-time adaptation for RAG. None of these have been applied to autoformalization or Lean 4. (5) Static retrieval and error analysis for autoformalization: DDR builds a 500K-sample dependency dataset and quantifies that ~30% of ICL-generated dependencies are hallucinated identifiers (Hall_m ranging 0.21-0.39 across frontier LLMs), reduced to <2% with retrieval-based DDR. DRIFT (ICLR 2026) achieves 62.33% BEq+@10 on Con-NF but falls short on ProofNet (21.93% vs 27.54%). CRAMF indexes 26K+ Mathlib definitions for concept-level retrieval, documenting that models fabricate identifiers like 'Function.Continuous' instead of 'ContinuousOn' and 'Group.index' instead of 'Subgroup.index'. MathAtlas (May 2026) introduces 52K graduate-level problems where the best model achieves only 2.6% on MA-Hard and adding local context degrades prompted systems' performance. The RAutoformalizer (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) explicitly categorizes compilation errors into 'Hallucination' (identifier hallucination) vs 'Others', establishing that identifier-related errors constitute a major error class. After exhaustive search through May 2026, no work combines (a) co-adaptive retrieval exploiting Lean 4's structured error taxonomy during test-time RL, (b) a calibrated semantic critic as RL reward with distributional shift analysis, (c) principled adaptation of binary-reward debiased RL to multi-tier rewards, and (d) test-time adaptation on fully unlabeled OOD domains.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide untried combination: 'Compilation-error-driven co-adaptive retrieval (R3/Reinforced-IR paradigm) exploiting Lean 4's full error taxonomy + calibrated CriticLean semantic critic reward + DDRL debiased advantages adapted to multi-tier rewards via GDPO-style binarize-then-enrich + Test-Time RL.' Also: evidence 'DDR shows ~30% of ICL-generated dependencies are hallucinated identifiers (Hall_m=0.21-0.39)' + evidence 'MathAtlas shows 66% advantage for Mathlib-grounded definitions and naive context injection degrades performance' + gap 'DDRL's binary debiasing has never been adapted to multi-tier rewards for autoformalization' + gap 'Lean 4's structured error taxonomy provides graded retrieval signals that no work exploits systematically' + gap 'CriticLean's accuracy on balanced benchmarks does not characterize OOD TTRL performance under skewed distributions' + pattern 'Alternating retriever-generator optimization (Reinforced-IR)' + insight 'GDPO shows standard GRPO collapses multi-reward signals into identical advantages.'",
  "approach": "We propose TTRA (Test-Time Retrieval-Augmented autoformalization), a framework that makes TTRL viable for autoformalization through three technical innovations: (1) a dual-loop architecture with co-adaptive retrieval exploiting Lean 4's full structured error taxonomy, (2) integration of CriticLean-14B as semantic RL reward with explicit calibration under distributional shift, and (3) a binarize-then-enrich adaptation of DDRL's binary debiasing to multi-tier rewards using GDPO's per-reward decoupled normalization.

**Phase -1 — Error Signal Coverage Micro-Analysis (2-3 days).** Before committing to the pipeline design, we quantify the retrieval signal coverage that Lean 4's error taxonomy provides on OOD domains. We compile 500 candidate formalizations from an existing model (e.g., FormaRL or Kimina-7B) on Con-NF (OOD) and 500 on MathAtlas MA-Hard, collecting all compilation error messages. We classify each error into the following hierarchy:
  (a) Tier 1 — Direct identifier signals: `lean.unknownIdentifier` (names the missing constant), `unknown namespace` (names the namespace). These provide direct, machine-parseable mapping from error to needed Mathlib dependency.
  (b) Tier 2 — Type-based signals: `type mismatch` (contains expected vs actual type signatures), `failed to synthesize instance` (names the typeclass). These provide weaker but still informative retrieval signals—type signatures can be matched against Mathlib's type index, and typeclass names map to specific Mathlib modules.
  (c) Tier 3 — Indirect signals: tactic failures, elaboration errors, syntax errors. These provide no direct retrieval signal but can serve as negative examples (confirming that retrieved dependencies were insufficient).
  Quantitative thresholds: If Tier 1 errors constitute ≥40% of compilation failures, the co-adaptive retrieval mechanism is well-supported as designed. If Tier 1 is 20-40%, we rely on both Tier 1 and Tier 2 signals (requiring the type-signature matching extension). If Tier 1 is <20%, we must fall back primarily to Tier 2 signals with type-signature-based retrieval. Prior evidence strongly supports ≥40%: DDR shows ~30% of ICL-generated dependencies are hallucinated identifiers (Hall_m=0.21-0.39 across frontier LLMs), the RAutoformalizer (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) treats 'Hallucination' (identifier hallucination) as one of two major error classes, and CRAMF documents systematic fabrication of close-but-wrong identifiers. Resource: ~8 A100-hours for generation, ~10 CPU-hours for compilation and error parsing. No model training required.

**Phase 0 — Minimal Pilot Experiment with Critic Calibration (De-risking).** Before committing to the full pipeline, we validate two riskiest assumptions with a minimal experiment. Setup: Take FormaRL's GRPO pipeline, replace its LLM-consistency reward with CriticLean-14B as the sole semantic reward signal (reward = r_compile × r_critic). Data: 200 problems from Con-NF (OOD) + 200 from FormalMATH number theory (near-distribution). No retrieval, no curriculum, no DDRL debiasing—just vanilla GRPO with the critic reward.
  Primary hypothesis: if CriticLean-14B reward achieves ≥3pp BEq@1 improvement over compilation-only GRPO on Con-NF, the core premise (semantic critic rewards enable OOD adaptation) is validated.
  Secondary hypothesis — Critic calibration under distributional shift: We explicitly measure CriticLean-14B's precision and recall SEPARATELY on the skewed distribution produced during TTRL. Specifically: (a) Among K=32 candidates per problem, record the number that compile and the number the critic approves. (b) For problems where <10% of candidates compile (the regime expected on hard OOD domains), manually inspect 100 random critic-approved candidates and 100 critic-rejected candidates to compute precision (what fraction of critic-approved candidates are semantically correct) and recall (what fraction of actually-correct candidates are approved). (c) Report calibration curves: for each critic confidence bin (if logit-based confidence is available from the critic model), plot the empirical correctness rate. Key concern: on CriticLeanBench's balanced 250/250 distribution, 84.8% accuracy could correspond to very different precision/recall trade-offs. Under OOD TTRL's heavily skewed distribution (90%+ incorrect), even moderate false positive rates could produce substantial noise. Our conservative binarization (requiring BOTH compile AND critic approval) inherently prioritizes precision over recall—a candidate must pass two independent filters. If critic precision on the skewed distribution is <80% (i.e., >20% of critic-approved compilable candidates are semantically wrong), we introduce critic confidence gating: only accept critic judgments with confidence >0.8, trading recall for precision.
  Resource: ~50 A100-hours (increased from 40 to include calibration analysis), 2-3 weeks. Go/no-go decision: proceed only if primary hypothesis confirmed AND critic precision on the skewed distribution ≥80% (or ≥80% with confidence gating).

**Phase 1 — Base Formalizer and Critic Integration.** Fine-tune a Qwen3-8B base model as a retrieval-augmented autoformalizer using DDR's 500K-sample dependency dataset and GRPO with the multi-tier reward function R(y, x) = r_compile × (α·r_critic + β·r_beq), where: r_compile ∈ {0,1} is the Lean 4 compilation gate (verified via Kimina Lean Server with 128 parallel pre-warmed REPL workers); r_critic ∈ {0,1} is the semantic fidelity judgment from CriticLeanGPT-Qwen3-14B-RL, gated by the confidence threshold established in Phase 0; r_beq ∈ [0,1] is the BEq consensus density (fraction of compilable candidates in the same BEq equivalence class). We set α=0.7, β=0.3 to weight semantic fidelity over syntactic consensus, since BEq has high precision (98.6%) but low recall (~33% on ProofNet). Adaptive reward degradation: when fewer than M=4 candidates out of K=32 compile, BEq becomes degenerate, and the reward falls back to R = r_compile × r_critic.

**Phase 2 — Dual-Loop Co-Adaptive Retrieval with Graded Error Signals (Core Innovation #1).** The retriever is a DDR-style dense encoder whose parameters ARE updated during TTRL—not frozen. This exploits a key structural property: Lean 4's type checker produces machine-parseable error messages with a hierarchy of retrieval informativeness.

  Loop 1 — Formalizer GRPO (every step): Generate K=32 candidate formalizations per problem, compile each against Lean 4, compute multi-tier rewards, and perform debiased GRPO updates (Phase 3).

  Loop 2 — Retriever contrastive update (every N_ret=50 GRPO steps): Accumulated compilation feedback generates contrastive training data for the retriever using a graded error signal hierarchy:
    (a) Tier 1 — Direct identifier signals (highest confidence): When a formalization fails with `lean.unknownIdentifier` (tagged with `unknownIdentifierMessageTag`), the error explicitly names the missing Mathlib constant (e.g., 'unknown identifier Finset.sum_comm'). The dependencies that WERE retrieved but did NOT include this constant are hard negatives. The missing constant—looked up in the CRAMF/DDR Mathlib constant index—becomes the positive example. When the error is `unknown namespace`, the namespace maps to a Mathlib module, providing a coarser positive signal.
    (b) Tier 2 — Type-based signals (moderate confidence): When a formalization fails with `type mismatch`, the error contains expected vs actual type signatures. We match these type signatures against Mathlib's type index (built from DDR's 500K-sample dataset) to identify candidate dependencies that would resolve the mismatch, generating softer positive examples with reduced weight (0.5× in the InfoNCE loss). When `failed to synthesize instance` names a typeclass, we retrieve Mathlib instances of that typeclass as positives.
    (c) Tier 3 — Negative confirmation from non-identifier errors: Tactic failures, elaboration errors, and syntax errors do not provide positive retrieval signals but confirm that the retrieved dependency set was insufficient for reasons beyond identifier resolution. These contribute only negative examples to the contrastive loss.
    (d) Positive confirmation from successful compilations: When a formalization compiles successfully, all retrieved Mathlib dependencies that appear in the compiled formalization are confirmed positives.
    (e) Weighted InfoNCE contrastive loss: L_InfoNCE = -Σ_k w_k · log(exp(sim(q, d_k+)/τ) / Σ_j exp(sim(q, d_j)/τ)), where w_k = 1.0 for Tier 1 positives, w_k = 0.5 for Tier 2 positives, w_k = 1.0 for compilation-confirmed positives, and τ is the temperature (initialized at 0.07).
    (f) Decoupled optimization: The retriever's gradient does NOT flow through the formalizer's policy gradient. This alternating optimization prevents instability, following R3 (NeurIPS 2025) and Reinforced-IR (ACL 2025). After each retriever update, the FAISS index over Mathlib dependency embeddings is rebuilt.

  The graded error signal hierarchy ensures the retriever update loop has sufficient signal even on the hardest OOD domains where pure unknownIdentifier errors may be sparse. Phase -1's micro-analysis determines the empirical signal mix, allowing the weighting scheme to be calibrated before full-scale experiments.

**Phase 3 — Binarize-Then-Enrich: Adapting DDRL to Multi-Tier Rewards (Core Innovation #2).** DDRL's three-component fix was designed for binary correct/incorrect rewards on informal math. Autoformalization's multi-tier reward has a continuous range. We adapt via binarize-then-enrich:

  (a) Binarization layer (for DDRL compatibility): Define binary acceptance r_accept = I(r_compile=1 AND r_critic=1). Compilation is a non-negotiable binary gate; the critic's precision (characterized in Phase 0 under distributional shift) makes it the most informative signal after compilation.
    - Balanced sampling: Partition K=32 candidates into 'accepted' (compile + critic approves) and 'rejected' (otherwise). Exclude problems where acceptance frequency is in the ambiguous zone (30-70%, i.e., ~10-22 of 32 accepted), following DDRL's insight that medium-consistency samples are the primary source of reward noise.
    - Fixed advantages: A_i = +1 for accepted candidates, A_i = -1 for rejected, eliminating GRPO's group-relative normalization that DDRL identifies as the amplification pathway.
    - Consensus-based off-policy refinement: After each TTRL epoch, sample M=128 formalizations per problem, apply acceptance filtering, perform rejection sampling on high-confidence samples (>80% acceptance rate), and run SFT on this high-quality dataset for 5 epochs.
  (b) GDPO-style enrichment layer (for BEq signal preservation): Among accepted candidates only, apply per-reward decoupled normalization for the BEq component. The BEq consensus density is normalized independently, preserving its ranking information without collapsing it into the binary acceptance signal. This adds an additive gradient bonus δ·norm(r_beq) to the fixed +1 advantage for accepted candidates, where δ=0.3 scales the enrichment relative to the debiased signal.
  (c) Methodological contribution: This binarize-then-enrich adaptation from single-reward to multi-tier debiased RL is applicable beyond autoformalization to any multi-tier reward where one component is continuous and others are binary.

**Phase 4 — Progressive Domain Curriculum for Test-Time Adaptation.** To break the bootstrapping problem (poor OOD retrieval → bad formalizations → noisy rewards → failed adaptation), we apply a progressive curriculum with quantitative transition criteria:

  (a) Near-distribution warm-start: TTRL on domains close to training data where retrieval coverage is high. Transition criterion (a)→(b): compilation rate ≥40%, critic approval rate ≥60% among compilable candidates, BEq@32 improves ≥3pp over pre-adaptation baseline. Timeout: T_max=500 GRPO steps.
  (b) Retrieval bootstrapping: Use the adapted model to generate improved formalization attempts on moderately OOD domains. Failed attempts with structured error signals (Tier 1 and Tier 2) feed the retriever's contrastive updates (Phase 2). Transition criterion (b)→(c): retrieval recall@10 ≥30% on bootstrapped queries, compilation rate on moderate-OOD ≥25%. Early transition: compilation rate plateaus (<2pp improvement over 200 consecutive steps).
  (c) Far-OOD adaptation: TTRL on truly OOD domains (algebraic geometry, condensed mathematics, MathAtlas MA-Hard) using the bootstrapped retriever and adaptive reward fallback (R = r_compile × r_critic when <4 candidates compile).

**Evaluation.** Measure BEq@K and compilation success on FormalMATH's 5,560-problem multi-domain benchmark, Con-NF, CombiBench, and MathAtlas's MA-Hard (700 entities, average dependency depth 30, best current model: 2.6%).
  Same-scale comparisons (primary, all ~7-8B parameter models): (1) FormaRL (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) as RL-without-retrieval baseline, (2) Online RL for Autoformalization (Wang et al.) as training-time RL baseline with composite rewards, (3) DRIFT with Qwen3-8B as strongest static retrieval baseline, (4) compilation-only TTRL and critic-only TTRL ablations, (5) standard GRPO vs. DDRL debiased vs. binarize-then-enrich (with separate ablations for each DDRL component and the GDPO enrichment layer), (6) frozen retriever vs. co-adaptive retriever during TTRL (isolating the value of compilation-error-driven retriever updates from natural query improvement), (7) Tier 1-only vs. Tier 1+2 vs. all-tier error signals (isolating the value of the graded error hierarchy), (8) no curriculum vs. progressive curriculum.
  Cross-scale reference points (for contextualizing absolute performance, NOT for claiming superiority): (9) ATF-32B as iterative refinement SOTA (94.51%/65.38% FormalMath-Lite/CombiBench), (10) ATLAS as SFT-only reference (70.08% pass@1 miniF2F), (11) Monotonic Refinement as inference-time orchestration upper bound (90.27% miniF2F, multi-model ensemble with GPT-4+ level models). All evaluation tables explicitly annotate model scale and compute budget to ensure fair interpretation.
  Sensitivity analysis: Dedicated ablation for N_ret ∈ {25, 50, 100} (retriever update frequency), as this controls the retriever-formalizer alternation and is critical for stability.",

**Phase 0 — Minimal Pilot Experiment with Critic Calibration (De-risking).** Before committing to the full pipeline, we validate two riskiest assumptions with a minimal experiment.   Secondary hypothesis — Critic calibration under distributional shift: We explicitly measure CriticLean-14B's precision and recall SEPARATELY on the skewed distribution produced during TTRL. Specifically: (a) Among K=32 candidates per problem, record the number that compile and the number the critic approves. (b) For problems where <10% of candidates compile (the regime expected on hard OOD domains), manually inspect 100 random critic-approved candidates and 100 critic-rejected candidates to compute precision (what fraction of critic-approved candidates are semantically correct) and recall (what fraction of actually-correct candidates are approved). Adaptive reward degradation: when fewer than M=4 candidates out of K=32 compile, BEq becomes degenerate, and the reward falls back to R = r_compile × r_critic.

This exploits a key structural property: Lean 4's type checker produces machine-parseable error messages with a hierarchy of retrieval informativeness.

  Loop 1 — Formalizer GRPO (every step): Generate K=32 candidate formalizations per problem, compile each against Lean 4, compute multi-tier rewards, and perform debiased GRPO updates (Phase 3).

  Loop 2 — Retriever contrastive update (every N_ret=50 GRPO steps): Accumulated compilation feedback generates contrastive training data for the retriever using a graded error signal hierarchy:

When the error is `unknown namespace`, the namespace maps to a Mathlib module, providing a coarser positive signal.
    (b) Tier 2 — Type-based signals (moderate confidence): When a formalization fails with `type mismatch`, the error contains expected vs actual type signatures. We match these type signatures against Mathlib's type index (built from DDR's 500K-sample dataset) to identify candidate dependencies that would resolve the mismatch, generating softer positive examples with reduced weight (0.5× in the InfoNCE loss). When `failed to synthesize instance` names a typeclass, we retrieve Mathlib instances of that typeclass as positives.
    (c) Tier 3 — Negative confirmation from non-identifier errors: Tactic failures, elaboration errors, and syntax errors do not provide positive retrieval signals but confirm that the retrieved dependency set was insufficient for reasons beyond identifier resolution. These contribute only negative examples to the contrastive loss.
    (d) Positive confirmation from successful compilations: When a formalization compiles successfully, all retrieved Mathlib dependencies that appear in the compiled formalization are confirmed positives.
    (e) Weighted InfoNCE contrastive loss: L_InfoNCE = -Σ_k w_k · log(exp(sim(q, d_k+)/τ) / Σ_j exp(sim(q, d_j)/τ)), where w_k = 1.0 for Tier 1 positives, w_k = 0.5 for Tier 2 positives, w_k = 1.0 for compilation-confirmed positives, and τ is the temperature (initialized at 0.07).
    (f) Decoupled optimization: The retriever's gradient does NOT flow through the formalizer's policy gradient. This alternating optimization prevents instability, following R3 (NeurIPS 2025) and Reinforced-IR (ACL 2025). After each retriever update, the FAISS index over Mathlib dependency embeddings is rebuilt.

  The graded error signal hierarchy ensures the retriever update loop has sufficient signal even on the hardest OOD domains where pure unknownIdentifier errors may be sparse. Phase -1's micro-analysis determines the empirical signal mix, allowing the weighting scheme to be calibrated before full-scale experiments.

  (a) Binarization layer (for DDRL compatibility): Define binary acceptance r_accept = I(r_compile=1 AND r_critic=1). Compilation is a non-negotiable binary gate; the critic's precision (characterized in Phase 0 under distributional shift) makes it the most informative signal after compilation.
    - Balanced sampling: Partition K=32 candidates into 'accepted' (compile + critic approves) and 'rejected' (otherwise). Exclude problems where acceptance frequency is in the ambiguous zone (30-70%, i.e., ~10-22 of 32 accepted), following DDRL's insight that medium-consistency samples are the primary source of reward noise.
